title: Pee Wee Erwin and the Kings of Jazz tours
summary: Leeman recalls working with Pee Wee Erwin from 1950 and touring Britain, Scandinavia and Germany with the Kings of Jazz, with Privin, Hyman, Holley, Hubble, Davern and Mince.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I'm gonna touch lightly upon my associations with some more wonderful musicians, and I'd like to get to Pee Wee Irwin -- I say touch lightly upon them because there are so many people to cover. Right now, I'm running out of tape.

Pee Wee Irwin -- of course, I first knew him when I was with -- when he was with the Tommy Dorsey Band, and in '39 along with Yank Lawson on trumpets and so forth and so on, and I -- when Bobby Hackett left Nick's that first year, I stayed on and this is 1950 -- I stayed on and Pee Wee Irwin became the leader, and I'd done much work and recordings and concerts with Pee Wee over the years. We've been more than friends. I went to Britain with Pee Wee; Scotland, England, London, Edinburgh, Stockholm, Sweden, Germany -- we played the German International Jazz Festival, this was only 3, 4 years ago, we played the International Jazz festival in Hanover, Germany; and we also rehearsed for four days in Iceland -- and I repeat, Iceland -- I don't know who booked that! But the office did when they brought us over to Europe, and I was with the group that Pee Wee was the leader of was called the Kings of Jazz. They named us that over in London -- the office did -- they thought that was apt.

It was some band; there was Bernie Privin, the guy I used to work with in the old Artie Shaw and Charlie Barnet days, and he had been in the studios for years; he's a wonderful trumpet player in the Louis Armstrong vein. Dick

Hyman was on piano with us and Major Holley on base; Ed Hubbie on trombone, Kenny Davern -- he played both the clarinet and primarily the soprano saxophone -- I have a mental block with that word 'soprano'.

However, on with the story. Kenny played that instrument just about as great as anybody alive today, that I know of. And I mentioned before that we had a little trio with Dick Wellstood, but that's beside the point. Johnny Mince played the clarinet -- Johnny had been in that Tommy Dorsey band in '39, too. It's funny that we all reunite after the years and after the many years in between to pursue our pursuits of music.

We played with the same group -- that group that I just mentioned, in concert in the states, too, from the Jersey Jazz Society, they brought us down, and recorded us, but it has never been released yet. I hope it will be someday; it's -- we were in jazz concerts in the states, too; we went down to Arkansas and so forth. And that's another group like the World's Greatest Jazz Band that we put together, and keep together.
I can't say enough about Pee Wee Irvin -- he's a great trumpet player, and we've been in constant contact over the years, and I do many concerts with him, so we're in personal contact at all times.
